source.title: The Truth Lies Somewhere in the Middle (of the Generated Tokens)
source.authors: Sophie L. Wang; Phillip Isola; Brian Cheung

page_placements.theme: Similarity estimates depend on invariances, dimension, extraction and preprocessing

record.tranche_reason: The study directly examines whether alignment results depend on the similarity measure and on preserving meaningful sample correspondence. It reports both robustness across CKA and m-kNN and cases where alignment disappears or is misleading under changed correspondence or biased CKA.
record.gate_note: The study measures alignment between a language model’s generated-token representations and fixed reference spaces; it does not test convergence as models scale or become more capable. Rows focus on reported metric and correspondence comparisons. The model-generated sample text and prompt examples are not instructions addressed to this study’s reader.
record.test_reason: The study uses PRH-style kernel alignment (debiased CKA, m-kNN) between Qwen3-14B hidden states and fixed DINOv2/ESM-3/gold-solution embeddings as a yardstick for embedding quality. It then compares ways of pooling generated-token hidden states. It never asks whether independently trained models converge, with scale or otherwise. Its metric and shuffling checks are sanity controls on its own pooling result, not tests of whether convergence claims depend on the metric or data. So it relies on the alignment finding as a tool and reports its own method's performance (T4).
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is off-target: it states a side point from the appendix. The authors conclude that mean pooling over generated-token hidden states gives more semantic representations than any single token or prompt-token pooling (CKA 0.410 vs 0.184). They find that mixing token segments, decoding seeds or views raises alignment, so semantic information is spread across the generation. They also find that alignment trajectories show interpretable phases tied to the model processing its own output. The m-kNN and biased-CKA material is offered only as metric-robustness justification.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates generated-token representations against fixed reference spaces, rather than testing model-to-model convergence with the original scale-and-alignment setup. It uses debiased CKA as its main measure and m-kNN as a corroborating measure.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment depends on preserving image-text correspondence and token order. Metric choice matters in the noise/shuffling controls: biased CKA can report increased alignment where debiased CKA does not. m-kNN is reported at k=10; the authors note its dependence on k but do not sweep k.

fits_no_version.finding: LLM-to-DINOv2 alignment depends strongly on how hidden states are extracted. Mean-pooled generated tokens score 0.410 versus 0.184 for prompt tokens (debiased CKA, WIT). Pooling rule also matters: 0.29–0.41.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Measured cross-modal alignment of a language model is highly sensitive to the representation-extraction choice (prompt vs generated tokens, pooling rule, layer), not only to the metric.

fits_no_version.finding: Biased CKA reports increased alignment under isotropic noise and shuffled pairings, while debiased CKA stays at baseline (App. A, Fig. 12).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Biased-CKA alignment values can be inflated with no real correspondence, so alignment estimates depend on estimator debiasing.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (PMLR 306, 2026)
record.problems: The core comparisons use a single main language model, a single WIT sample of 1024 examples, and m-kNN at k=10; the paper notes m-kNN sensitivity to k and sampling noise. Several relevant comparisons are shown only in figures without numeric values. No model-scale or capability sweep tests the central scale claim.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted due to the row cap. Retrieval, ranking, and clustering tables (Tables 3–5) were not included because they are downstream evaluations rather than direct tests of the metric/correspondence dependence recorded here.

untested.parts: All: no comparison of independently trained models across scale or capability.

All: one LLM is aligned to a fixed vision encoder to rank pooling rules. There is no systematic test of alignment rising as both models improve. A single Qwen3-8B vs 14B embedding comparison appears only in Fig. 20.
All: no seed-wise comparison of independently trained networks. 'Seeds' here are decoding seeds of one model.
All: no mapping, stitching or interchangeability test.
All: no feature or circuit universality test.
Not tested as a claim about convergence: there is no k sweep, no OOD inputs, and no test of whether cross-model convergence findings survive other metrics.
All: no test of plateau or of shared-data explanations.

missing.what: Same generations embedded by Qwen3-8B vs Qwen3-14B. The text states the higher-capacity model gives better-aligned embeddings overall, with the same qualitative curve. Figure only, no numbers, a single size pair. This is weak, incidental evidence on capacity and cross-modal alignment, not a designed test.

Alignment with additional vision encoders (DINOv3, ViT-MAE, ViT-MSN) and additional LLMs (Qwen3-8B, OLMo3-7B, gpt-oss-20B). Figure only. These are pooling-robustness checks, but they hold cross-model alignment levels that a V1/V2 comparison might want.

record.verdict_notes: The study uses alignment as a yardstick for embedding extraction, not as an object of study, so no verdicts are given. The reader's V6 'supports' labels confuse sanity controls (shuffled pairings collapse alignment) with evidence that convergence findings depend on the metric. The reader's 'limits_scope' label rests on the authors' own pooling-method comparisons. Authors are PRH coauthors (Isola, Cheung), but this is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No test of alignment between independently trained models as model size or capability increases.
Uses image-caption/reference alignment, but does not test whether alignment between vision and language models rises as both improve.
No comparison of independently initialized networks of the same architecture or their shared features/subspaces.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability test between models.
No test of recurring interpretable features or circuits across models.
Tests debiased CKA versus m-kNN at k=10, and tests altered sample correspondence. It does not sweep k, broadly vary the datasets or input distributions, or test out-of-distribution inputs.
Does not test whether cross-model alignment plateaus or is explained by shared training data or objectives.

rows.subject: Qwen3-14B
rows.operation_detail: Compared alignment after isotropic noise perturbations around the token-mean representation with the unperturbed mean.
rows.uncertainty: Distribution over 100 perturbations; numerical uncertainty not stated
rows.note: The text says the unperturbed mean has higher alignment than the noisy perturbations when correspondence is preserved.
rows.check: Noise-perturbation control testing whether the pooling gain is mere variance reduction. It is about the authors' method, not cross-model convergence.

rows.subject: Qwen3-14B
rows.operation_detail: Compared alignment after isotropic noise perturbations around the token-mean representation with the unperturbed mean after shuffling image-text pairings.
rows.uncertainty: Distribution over 100 perturbations; numerical uncertainty not stated
rows.note: The text says the improvement disappears when semantic correspondence is broken.
rows.check: Shuffled-pairing sanity control: the pooling gain vanishes without correspondence. This is expected for any alignment measure and says nothing on V6's metric or input dependence of convergence.

rows.subject: Qwen3-14B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated noisy and shuffled-correspondence alignment using biased CKA.
rows.note: The text states that biased CKA can show increased alignment despite broken correspondence or added noise.
rows.check: Biased CKA shows inflated alignment under noise or shuffling. This replicates a known estimator bias the authors cite (Davari 2023; Murphy 2024) to justify their metric. It is recorded under fits_no_version, not as a V6 test.

rows.subject: Qwen3-14B
rows.baseline: random-kernel alignment; numerical value not stated
rows.locator: Appendix A, Figure 12; Appendix C, Figures 15–16
rows.note: The text says interior simplex maxima disappear when correspondence is broken.
rows.check: Shuffled-correspondence control for the simplex result. It is a sanity check, not a convergence measurement.

rows.subject: Qwen3-14B
rows.operation_detail: Compared tokenwise alignment after shuffling token embeddings with alignment in their original temporal order.
rows.note: The text says shuffling removes the phase structure and converts prefix averaging to averaging over randomly ordered tokens; the monotonic prefix trend depends on token order.
rows.check: Token-order ablation of the authors' prefix-averaging curve. It does not bear on convergence between models.

rows.subject: Qwen3-14B
rows.operation_detail: Shuffled generated tokens before re-embedding, changing the autoregressive computation.
rows.note: The text states alignment is reduced but remains above chance.
rows.check: Re-embedding ablation of token order. It is internal to the pooling analysis.

rows.subject: Qwen3-14B
rows.operation_detail: Shuffled sample pairings during kernel alignment.
rows.baseline: alignment expected between random kernels; numerical value not stated
rows.note: The text says alignment collapses to that expected between random kernels.
rows.check: Shuffled-pairing control (alignment drops to random-kernel level). It is a sanity check.

rows.subject: Qwen3-14B
rows.operation_detail: Compared tokenwise and token-slice convex-combination alignment under m-kNN with the corresponding qualitative patterns under debiased CKA.
rows.uncertainty: Across five seeds: mean standard deviation 2.3 × 10−3; maximum 5.7 × 10−3
rows.note: The text reports that mean pooling and interior token-slice mixtures retain the qualitative CKA patterns under m-kNN.
rows.check: Shows the authors' pooling and simplex patterns hold under m-kNN k=10. This is robustness of their own method's ranking, not of a convergence claim.

relation.reason: Uses representational-alignment methodology as a semantic-quality yardstick with fixed reference embeddings; does not test convergence with scale, training seeds, or interchangeable representations.

tranche.reason: Uses reference-space alignment to evaluate embedding extraction methods. The pooling comparisons and metric controls do not test the catalog's convergence claims.

source_check.notes: Section 3.3 explicitly reports 0.410 versus 0.184; Table 2 reports 0.4106, 0.2910, 0.2932 and 0.3505. These method comparisons, including the selected best-token value, should remain outside convergence-evidence rows.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Shuffled image-text correspondence and token-order controls
reader_labels.reason: Alignment disappears with shuffled pairings, while token-order shuffling disrupts the trajectory trend; this shows dependence on correspondence and input arrangement (r10, r12–r15).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Biased CKA under noise or broken correspondence
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports that biased CKA can increase alignment even when noise or shuffled pairings remove meaningful correspondence (r11).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Meaningful WIT correspondence under debiased CKA and m-kNN at k=10
reader_labels.reason: The qualitative pooling and token-slice alignment trends persist across these two metrics, so the reported effect does not vanish under this tested alternative metric (r1–r8, r16).
